claim: i-CDK9 has a N2′-(trans-4-aminocyclohexyl)-5′-chloro-N6-(3-fluorobenzyl)-2,4′-bipyridine-2′,6-diamine scaffold that is structurally distinct from flavopiridol and all the other known non-selective CDK inhibitors
source: i-CDK9 has a N2′-(trans-4-aminocyclohexyl)-5′-chloro-N6-(3-fluorobenzyl)-2,4′-bipyridine-2′,6-diamine scaffold that is structurally distinct from flavopiridol and all the other known non-selective CDK inhibitors (Figure 1A).
evidence: The chemical structure is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text as distinct from known inhibitors.

claim: i-CDK9 occupies the ATP-binding pocket of the CDK9 kinase domain as revealed by a co-crystal structure solved at 2.6 Å resolution
source: It occupies the ATP-binding pocket of the CDK9 kinase domain as revealed by a co-crystal structure solved at 2.6 Å resolution (manuscript in preparation).
evidence: The text states that a co-crystal structure at 2.6 Å resolution reveals the binding mode, though the full manuscript is in preparation.

claim: i-CDK9 potently inhibits the CDK9-CycT1 catalytic activity with an IC50 value below the detection limit of 0.0004 µM
source: Using an in vitro AlphaScreen (PerkinElmer, Inc)-based kinase assay, i-CDK9 was shown to potently inhibit the CDK9-CycT1 catalytic activity with an IC50 value below the detection limit of 0.0004 µM (Figure 1B).
evidence: The IC50 value is determined by an in vitro kinase assay and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Flavopiridol showed an IC50 value of 0.007 µM against CDK9-CycT1 in the AlphaScreen-based kinase assay
source: In the same assay, flavopiridol showed an IC50 value of 0.007 µM.
evidence: The IC50 value is measured in the same assay as i-CDK9.

claim: i-CDK9 exhibited at least 600-fold lower activity toward CDK1-CycB, CDK2-CycA, CDK4-CycD1, CDK7-CycH-MAT1 and CDK8-CycC compared to its inhibition of CDK9-CycT1
source: Furthermore, compared to its inhibition of the CDK9-CycT1 kinase activity, i-CDK9 exhibited at least 600-fold lower activity toward CDK1-CycB, CDK2-CycA, CDK4-CycD1, CDK7-CycH-MAT1 and CDK8-CycC (Figure 1B).
evidence: The selectivity is demonstrated by comparing IC50 values in the same assay system, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Flavopiridol displayed only 2.9- to 28.6-fold lower activity toward CDK1-CycB, CDK2-CycA, CDK4-CycD1, CDK7-CycH-MAT1 and CDK8-CycC compared to CDK9-CycT1
source: In contrast, flavopiridol displayed only 2.9- to 28.6-fold lower activity toward the same CDK-cyclin pairs compared to CDK9-CycT1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The selectivity profile is determined by comparing IC50 values in the same assay, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At 1 µM, i-CDK9 almost completely blocked the binding of CDK9 to the immobilized ligands (only 5.1% CDK9 captured on solid support)
source: At 1 µM, i-CDK9 almost completely blocked the binding of CDK9 to the immobilized ligands (only 5.1% CDK9 captured on solid support; Figure 1A)
evidence: The binding inhibition is measured using the KINOMEscan assay platform and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: i-CDK9 displayed essentially no effect on CDK5 (100% binding to immobilized ligands), CDK11 (94%), CDK13 (100%) and only a partial inhibition of the binding of CDK3 (57%)
source: but displayed essentially no effect on CDK5 (100% binding to immobilized ligands), CDK11 (94%), CDK13 (100%) and only a partial inhibition of the binding of CDK3 (57%).
evidence: The selectivity is measured using the KINOMEscan binding assay at 1 µM i-CDK9.

claim: CDK12 phosphorylates the Pol II CTD on Ser2
source: Among all members of the CDK super family, CDK12 deserves special attention because of its reported phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD on Ser2, an ability that is shared with CDK9 (Bartkowiak et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bartkowiak et al., 2010.

claim: Ser2 phosphorylation by CDK9-F was efficiently inhibited by i-CDK9 with an estimated IC50 of ∼2 nM
source: While Ser2 phosphorylation by CDK9-F was efficiently inhibited by i-CDK9 with an estimated IC50 of ∼2 nM under the current experimental conditions, no obvious inhibition of CDK12-F was detected even at 80 nM of the inhibitor (Figure 1C).
evidence: The IC50 is estimated from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No obvious inhibition of CDK12-F was detected even at 80 nM of i-CDK9
source: While Ser2 phosphorylation by CDK9-F was efficiently inhibited by i-CDK9 with an estimated IC50 of ∼2 nM under the current experimental conditions, no obvious inhibition of CDK12-F was detected even at 80 nM of the inhibitor (Figure 1C).
evidence: The lack of inhibition is shown by in vitro kinase assays in Figure 1C.

claim: Ser2 phosphorylation by CDK9-CycT1 was mostly inhibited by 80 nM i-CDK9, while CDK12-CycK was not significantly inhibited until 640-1200 nM i-CDK9 was added
source: While Ser2 phosphorylation by CDK9-CycT1 was mostly inhibited by 80 nM i-CDK9, CDK12-CycK was not significantly inhibited until 640-1200 nM i-CDK9 was added into the reactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The differential inhibition is shown by in vitro kinase assays using recombinant proteins in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: i-CDK9 displayed markedly higher selectivity against CDK9 compared to CDK12
source: Thus, between CDK9 and CDK12, i-CDK9 displayed markedly higher selectivity against the former.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vitro kinase assay data comparing inhibition of CDK9 vs CDK12.

claim: Flavopiridol shows similar selectivity for CDK9 over CDK12 as i-CDK9
source: It is interesting to note that a similar finding has also been made with the pan-CDK inhibitor flavopiridol (Bosken et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bosken et al., 2014.

claim: Among >400 kinases evaluated in the KINOMEscan platform, only 9 consistently showed less than 40% binding to the immobilized ligands in the presence of 1 or 10 µM of i-CDK9
source: Among the >400 kinases evaluated, only 9 (highlighted yellow in Figure 1—source data 1) consistently showed less than 40% binding to the immobilized ligands in the presence of 1 or 10 µM of i-CDK9.
evidence: The selectivity profile is determined by the KINOMEscan platform and shown in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: i-CDK9 displayed great selectivity for CDK9 with more than 100-fold difference detected between CDK9 and the next two best targets DYRK1A and DYRK1B (IC50 < 0.0004 µM for CDK9 vs IC50 = 0.055 and 0.047 for DYRK1A and B, respectively)
source: Again, i-CDK9 was found to display great selectivity for CDK9 with more than 100-fold difference detected between CDK9 and the next two best targets DYRK1A and DYRK1B (IC50 < 0.0004 µM for CDK9 vs IC50 = 0.055 and 0.047 for DYRK1A and B, respectively; column D in Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The selectivity is determined by functional kinase assays or binding assays, with data shown in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: DYRK1A acts as a Pol II CTD Kinase at its target gene promoters
source: Indeed, it has recently been reported that DYRK1A acts as a Pol II CTD Kinase at its target gene promoters (Di Vona et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Vona et al., 2015.

claim: i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells
source: Consistent with its specific binding to and potent inhibition of purified CDK9-CycT1 in vitro, i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD and Thr775 (pThr775) in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The dose-dependent reduction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claim: i-CDK9 markedly reduced Thr775 phosphorylation in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells
source: Consistent with its specific binding to and potent inhibition of purified CDK9-CycT1 in vitro, i-CDK9 markedly reduced the CDK9-mediated pSer2 in the Pol II CTD and Thr775 (pThr775) in the DSIF subunit SPT5 in a dose-dependent manner in HeLa cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: The dose-dependent reduction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claim: i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1
source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The down-regulation is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claim: i-CDK9 induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)
source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The PARP cleavage is shown by Western blotting in Figure 1D.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of PARP is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation
source: Indeed, correlating with the decrease in cellular levels of pSer2 and pThr775, i-CDK9 markedly down-regulated the expression of the short-lived anti-apoptotic protein MCL-1 and at the same time induced proteolytic cleavage of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which is considered a major hallmark of apoptosis and caspase activation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Among the total of 11,197 genes with detectable Pol II peaks, 7805 (70%) showed a traveling ratio (TR) greater than 2.0 in the control DMSO-treated HeLa cells
source: Similar to the situation reported in other cell types (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Rahl et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2013), among the total of 11,197 genes with detectable Pol peaks, 7805 (70%) showed a traveling ratio (TR; also called the pausing index; (Zeitlinger et al., 2007; Rahl et al., 2010) greater than 2.0 in the control DMSO-treated HeLa cells.
evidence: The TR values are calculated from ChIP-seq data and compared to published findings in other cell types.

claim: Upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 hr, 6339 (56.6%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR
source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B)
evidence: The TR changes are determined by ChIP-seq analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 8 hr, 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR
source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B)
evidence: The TR changes are determined by ChIP-seq analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The increase in Pol II TR upon i-CDK9 treatment indicates significantly elevated promoter-proximal pausing by Pol II upon CDK9 inhibition
source: Importantly, upon treatment with i-CDK9 for 2 and 8 hr, 6339 (56.6%) and 7658 (68.4%) genes displayed an increase of at least 1.5-fold in Pol II TR, respectively (Figure 2B), indicating significantly elevated promoter-proximal pausing by Pol II upon CDK9 inhibition.
evidence: The interpretation is based on the definition of TR and the ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: TR values for the 138 genes whose expression was up-regulated at least twofold by i-CDK9 were significantly less affected compared to the rest of the genes
source: A comparison between the two data sets indicates that TR values for those 138 genes whose expression was up-regulated at least twofold by i-CDK9 were significantly less affected compared to the rest of the genes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The comparison is made between ChIP-seq and microarray data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The top 4 gene sets with the largest increase in TR show an enrichment in biological processes ranging from RNA processing, DNA and non-coding RNA metabolic process to transcription
source: Furthermore, the top 4 gene sets with the largest increase in TR show an enrichment in biological processes ranging from RNA processing, DNA and non-coding RNA metabolic process to transcription (Figure 2E).
evidence: The enrichment is determined by GO analysis using DAVID and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The top 4 gene sets whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process
source: Largely consistent with this TR-based analysis, the top 4 sets, whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment, are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process
evidence: The enrichment is determined by GO analysis using DAVID.

claim: Transcription regulation and RNA metabolic processes are particularly susceptible to inhibition of CDK9
source: Largely consistent with this TR-based analysis, the top 4 sets, whose expression had the biggest drop upon i-CDK9 treatment, are populated by genes involved in regulation of transcription and RNA metabolic process, indicating that these processes and their control are particularly susceptible to inhibition of CDK9.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the GO enrichment analysis of genes most affected by i-CDK9.

claim: MYC expression in i-CDK9-treated HeLa cells displayed a biphasic response with a small initial decrease (within 2 hr) followed by a dramatic rebound (around 8 hr and continue at 16 hr)
source: Microarray analysis performed at three different time points (2, 8 and 16 hr) indicates that MYC expression in i-CDK9-treated HeLa cells displayed an interesting biphasic responses with a small initial decrease (within 2 hr) followed by a dramatic rebound (around 8 hr and continue at 16 hr) in the presence of continuous CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The biphasic response is shown by microarray analysis at multiple time points in Figure 3A.

claim: The biphasic MYC expression pattern in response to i-CDK9 was confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis
source: This result was further confirmed by qRT-PCR analysis of MYC mRNA levels in cells treated with i-CDK9 or DMSO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The confirmation is provided by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A similar biphasic MYC expression pattern was observed in four other cell lines (U87MG, A375, NCIH441, and A2058) representing a wide spectrum of human cancers and MYC amplification states
source: In addition to HeLa cells, a similar biphasic expression pattern was also observed in four other cell lines representing a wide spectrum of human cancers and MYC amplification states (Figure 3A; http://www.broadinstitute.org/ccle/home).
evidence: The biphasic pattern is shown by microarray analysis in multiple cell lines in Figure 3A.

claim: The extent of the initial decrease and subsequent induction of MYC mRNA production varied among the cell lines
source: Notably, the extent of the initial decrease and then subsequent induction of MYC mRNA production varied among the cell lines.
evidence: This observation is based on comparing the microarray data from different cell lines.

claim: After 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, the MYC mRNA levels in U87MG and HeLa cells showed only a slight decrease compared to the DMSO control
source: For example, after 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, the MYC mRNA levels in U87MG (MYC copy number [CN] = 2) and HeLa (CN = 4) cells showed only a slight decrease compared to the DMSO control
evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: After 2 hr of i-CDK9 (0.5 µM) treatment, MYC mRNA levels were significantly reduced in A375, NCIH441, and A2058 cells
source: whereas they were significantly reduced in A375 (CN = 2), NCIH441 (CN = 8), and A2058 (CN = 4) cells.
evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: Prolonged treatment for 8–16 hr caused the MYC mRNA to reach levels much higher than those in the control cells in all cell lines except NCIH441
source: Furthermore, the prolonged treatment for 8–16 hr caused the MYC mRNA to reach levels much higher than those in the control cells in all cell lines except NCIH441 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: The induction of MYC expression in response to prolonged CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 is a general phenomenon likely caused by a common mechanism independent of the MYC amplification/expression levels
source: Despite these variations, which could well be caused by differences in MYC mRNA stability in difference cell lines, it is clear that the induction of MYC expression in response to prolonged CDK9 inhibition by i-CDK9 is a general phenomenon likely caused by a common mechanism independent of the MYC amplification/expression levels.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation of similar patterns across multiple cell lines with different MYC copy numbers.

claim: HEXIM1 was continuously suppressed throughout the entire 16 hr of i-CDK9 treatment in all five cell lines
source: In contrast to MYC, another short-lived gene HEXIM1, which was previously shown to depend on active CDK9 for expression (He et al., 2006), was continuously suppressed throughout the entire 16 hr of i-CDK9 treatment in all five cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The continuous suppression is shown by microarray analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and the CDK9 dependence is supported by citation to He et al., 2006.

claim: Upon exposure to 0.1 µM i-CDK9, the MYC level increased 3.6-fold whereas the global pSer2 level was only decreased by 23%
source: Upon exposure to just 0.1 µM i-CDK9, the MYC level increased 3.6-fold whereas the global pSer2 level was only decreased by 23% (Figure 3B).
evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting and quantified in Figure 3B.

claim: It took 1.0 µM i-CDK9 to cause up to 85% reduction in pSer2
source: It took 1.0 µM i-CDK9 to cause up to 85% reduction in pSer2.
evidence: This is measured by Western blotting and quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 8-hr incubation with i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced the MYC level by 3.3-fold, whereas the same condition reduced the pSer2 level by only 40%
source: In a separate time-course analysis, the 8-hr incubation with i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced the MYC level by 3.3-fold, whereas the same condition reduced the pSer2 level by only 40% (Figure 3C).
evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting and quantified in Figure 3C.

claim: MYC expression was highly responsive to i-CDK9 treatment and occurred at a time point earlier and drug concentration lower than those required to achieve a significant suppression of Ser2 phosphorylation on the Pol II CTD
source: Thus, MYC expression was highly responsive to i-CDK9 treatment and occurred at a time point earlier and drug concentration lower than those required to achieve a significant suppression of Ser2 phosphorylation on the Pol II CTD.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the dose-response and time-course data in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Flavopiridol significantly elevated the MYC protein level and this effect required a shorter exposure time (e.g., 4 hr) and lower drug concentration (e.g., 0.1 μM) than those needed to fully reduce the global pSer2 level
source: Just like i-CDK9, flavopiridol also significantly elevated the MYC protein level and this effect required a shorter exposure time (e.g., 4 hr) and lower drug concentration (e.g., 0.1 μM) than those needed to fully reduce the global pSer2 level (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: The protein levels are measured by Western blotting in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The nearly identical activities displayed by i-CDK9 and flavopiridol suggest that the inhibition of CDK9 but not some other unknown enzymes was the cause of MYC induction
source: The nearly identical activities displayed by i-CDK9 and flavopiridol, which are very different in their structures, suggest that the inhibition of CDK9 but not some other unknown enzymes was the cause of MYC induction.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the similar effects of two structurally distinct CDK9 inhibitors.

claim: Without cycloheximide pre-treatment, i-CDK9 significantly increased the MYC protein level
source: Without the pre-treatment, i-CDK9 significantly increased the MYC protein level as expected (Figure 3F, lanes 1–2).
evidence: The protein level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 3F.

claim: In the presence of cycloheximide, MYC production was essentially wiped out in both the i-CDK9-treated and i-CDK9-untreated cells
source: In the presence of CHX, however, MYC production was essentially wiped out in both the i-CDK9-treated and i-CDK9-untreated cells (lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: The protein level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 3F.

claim: MYC is a labile protein
source: This result, together with the above demonstration that sustained i-CDK9 treatment dramatically increased the MYC mRNA level (Figure 3A), indicates that MYC is a labile protein
evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide experiment showing rapid loss of MYC protein when synthesis is blocked.

claim: The prominent accumulation of MYC in i-CDK9-treated cells was most likely due to its enhanced mRNA production but not protein stability
source: This result, together with the above demonstration that sustained i-CDK9 treatment dramatically increased the MYC mRNA level (Figure 3A), indicates that MYC is a labile protein and that its prominent accumulation in i-CDK9-treated cells was most likely due to its enhanced mRNA production but not protein stability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combination of mRNA level data and cycloheximide experiment results.

claim: i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus
source: Interestingly, although i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus, it failed to activate production of the Flag-tagged MYC (MYC-F) from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter (Figure 3G)
evidence: The differential induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 3G.

claim: i-CDK9 failed to activate production of Flag-tagged MYC from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter
source: Interestingly, although i-CDK9 efficiently induced expression from the endogenous MYC locus, it failed to activate production of the Flag-tagged MYC (MYC-F) from a stably transfected, doxycycline-inducible expression construct driven by the CMV promoter (Figure 3G)
evidence: The lack of induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 3G.

claim: i-CDK9 cannot activate MYC transcription from the heterologous CMV promoter
source: indicating that i-CDK9 cannot activate MYC transcription from this heterologous promoter.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that i-CDK9 induces endogenous MYC but not CMV-driven MYC.

claim: i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F in a dosage-dependent manner
source: Indeed, i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F and at the same time increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: The protein-protein interactions are measured by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claim: i-CDK9 increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner
source: Indeed, i-CDK9 gradually decreased the amounts of HEXIM1 bound to CDK9-F and at the same time increased the BRD4-CDK9-F binding in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: The protein-protein interactions are measured by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claim: The disruption of 7SK snRNP and formation of BRD4-P-TEFb were highly sensitive to i-CDK9 and required as little as 0.1 μM of the drug
source: Just like the induction of MYC expression (Figure 3B), the disruption of 7SK snRNP and formation of BRD4-P-TEFb were highly sensitive to i-CDK9 and required as little as 0.1 μM of the drug (Figure 4A, compare lane 8 to lane 6).
evidence: The sensitivity is shown by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: At 0.1 μM i-CDK9, the global pSer2 level was only slightly decreased
source: At this concentration, i-CDK9 only slightly decreased the global pSer2 level (Figure 4A, compare between lanes 1 and 3) but began to markedly induce MYC expression (Figure 3B).
evidence: The pSer2 level is measured by Western blotting in Figure 4A.

claim: i-CDK9 (0.3 μM) induced disruption of 7SK snRNP at a time point (1 hr) that was much earlier than that required to cause about 50% reduction in global pSer2 (8 hr)
source: In a time course analysis, i-CDK9 (0.3 μM)-induced disruption of 7SK snRNP at a time point (1 hr) that was much earlier than that required to cause about 50% reduction in global pSer2 (8 hr; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The time course is shown by co-immunoprecipitation and Western blotting in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of BRD4 dramatically reduced both basal and the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production
source: The loss of BRD4, verified by Western blotting, dramatically reduced both basal and the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production (Figure 4B).
evidence: The effect of BRD4 knockdown is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4B.

claim: JQ1 decreased the associations of both BRD4 and CDK9 with the MYC locus in HeLa cells
source: Consistent with the results obtained in other cell types (Mertz et al., 2011; Zuber et al., 2011), JQ1 decreased the associations of both BRD4 and CDK9 with the MYC locus in HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The decreased associations are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and the consistency with other cell types is supported by citations to Mertz et al., 2011 and Zuber et al., 2011.

claim: JQ1 completely abolished the MYC induction by i-CDK9 in HeLa, H1792, and A2058 cells
source: More importantly, JQ1 also completely abolished the MYC induction by i-CDK9 in HeLa (Figure 4C) as well as the lung cancer cell line H1792 and the melanoma cell line A2058 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The abolishment of MYC induction is shown by Western blotting or qRT-PCR in Figures 4C and 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The control enantiomer of JQ1 was ineffective in abolishing MYC induction by i-CDK9
source: whereas the control enantiomer was ineffective in this regard.
evidence: The lack of effect is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4C.

claim: The interaction between BRD4 and acetylated chromatin is required for i-CDK9 to induce MYC expression in diverse cell types
source: These observations, in conjunction with the shBRD4 result above, confirm that the interaction between BRD4 and acetylated chromatin is required for i-CDK9 to induce MYC expression in diverse cell types.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of BRD4 knockdown and JQ1 treatment experiments in multiple cell lines.

claim: The overexpressed P-TEFb-interacting domain (PID) of BRD4 efficiently suppressed the i-CDK9-induced MYC protein production
source: Western analyses indicate that the PID efficiently suppressed the induction (Figure 4D, lanes 3 and 4)
evidence: The suppression is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4D.

claim: The PID strongly interacted with CDK9 and CycT1 in i-CDK9-treated cells
source: likely due to its own strong interaction with CDK9 and CycT1 in i-CDK9-treated cells (Figure 4E)
evidence: The interaction is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4E.

claim: The PID interfered with the interaction of endogenous BRD4 with P-TEFb
source: which in turn interfered with the interaction of endogenous BRD4 with P-TEFb (Figure 4F).
evidence: The interference is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4F.

claim: The overexpressed kinase-inactive CDK9 mutant D167N prevented i-CDK9 from inducing MYC
source: This point is illustrated by the demonstration that the overexpressed kinase-inactive CDK9 mutant D167N, which binds to BRD4-like WT CDK9 (Yang et al., 2005) and acts dominant-negatively to suppress the activity of endogenous CDK9 (Garber et al., 2000), prevented i-CDK9 from inducing MYC (Figure 4D, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: The prevention is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4D, and the properties of D167N are supported by citations to Yang et al., 2005 and Garber et al., 2000.

claim: The initial MYC induction by a low level (e.g., 0.3 μM) of i-CDK9 was subsequently shut off by a higher i-CDK9 concentration (e.g., 2 μM)
source: The dependence on catalytically active P-TEFb for MYC induction was further demonstrated by the observation that the initial MYC induction by a low level (e.g., 0.3 μM) of i-CDK9 was subsequently shut off by a higher i-CDK9 concentration (e.g., 2 μM, see Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The shut-off is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: No MYC induction was detected when 2 μM i-CDK9 was added into the medium at time zero
source: No MYC induction was detected also when 2 μM i-CDK9 was added into the medium at time zero (see Figure 7A below).
evidence: The lack of induction is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7A.

claim: The RNAi-mediated knockdown of cellular CDK9 and CycT1 levels completely abolished the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression
source: Finally, the RNAi-mediated KD of cellular CDK9 and CycT1 levels also completely abolished the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression (Figure 4G).
evidence: The abolishment is shown by Western blotting in Figure 4G.

claim: Knockdown of CDK12 failed to prevent i-CDK9 from inducing MYC
source: In contrast, KD of CDK12, another reported CTD kinase, failed to prevent i-CDK9 from inducing MYC (Figure 4H).
evidence: The lack of effect is shown by Western blotting and qRT-PCR in Figure 4H.

claim: The i-CDK9 induction of MYC expression depends on the enhanced interaction of BRD4 with catalytically active P-TEFb released from 7SK snRNP as well as the binding of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to acetylated MYC chromatin template
source: Taken together, these data strongly support the notion that the i-CDK9 induction of MYC expression depends on the enhanced interaction of BRD4 with catalytically active P-TEFb released from 7SK snRNP as well as the binding of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to acetylated MYC chromatin template.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of multiple experiments including knockdowns, inhibitors, and mutants.

claim: WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold
source: While WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold, ∆PID lacked this ability (Figure 4I)
evidence: The increase in kinase activity is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4I.

claim: BRD4∆PID lacked the ability to increase CDK9 kinase activity
source: While WT BRD4 was able to increase CDK9 kinase activity dose dependently up to 2.2-fold, ∆PID lacked this ability (Figure 4I)
evidence: The lack of effect is shown by in vitro kinase assays in Figure 4I.

claim: The physical interaction between BRD4 and P-TEFb is essential for the elevated CDK9 activity
source: indicating that the physical interaction between BRD4 and P-TEFb was essential for the elevated CDK9 activity.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the effects of WT BRD4 and ∆PID on CDK9 activity.

claim: Neither WT nor ∆PID BRD4 alone was able to cause phosphorylation of the CTD peptide in the absence of P-TEFb
source: It is worth pointing out that different from a recent study reporting that BRD4 is an atypical kinase that can directly phosphorylate the Pol II CTD on Ser2 (Devaiah et al., 2012), neither WT nor ∆PID BRD4 alone was able to cause phosphorylation of the CTD peptide in the absence of P-TEFb (Figure 4I).
evidence: The lack of kinase activity is shown by in vitro kinase assays in Figure 4I, and the contrast with another study is supported by citation to Devaiah et al., 2012.

claim: BRD4 rendered CDK9 less sensitive to inhibition by i-CDK9
source: In addition to increasing CDK9's catalytic activity, BRD4 was also found to render CDK9 less sensitive to inhibition by i-CDK9, whereas BRD4∆PID was less effective in this regard (Figure 4J).
evidence: The protection against inhibition is shown by in vitro kinase assays with varying i-CDK9 concentrations in Figure 4J.

claim: In the absence of BRD4, it took only 4.4 ± 0.7 nM i-CDK9 to achieve 50% inhibition of CDK9
source: For example, in the absence of BRD4, it took only 4.4 ± 0.7 nM i-CDK9 to achieve 50% inhibition of CDK9 (i.e., IC50 = 4.4 ± 0.7 nM).
evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The addition of WT BRD4 into the reaction protected CDK9 against i-CDK9 and increased IC50 to 14.7 ± 2.1 nM
source: However, the addition of WT BRD4 into the reaction protected CDK9 against i-CDK9 and increased IC50 to 14.7 ± 2.1 nM.
evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claim: BRD4∆PID changed the IC50 value to 7.2 ± 0.6 nM
source: BRD4∆PID, on the other hand, displayed a much weaker effect by changing the IC50 value to 7.2 ± 0.6 nM (Figure 4J).
evidence: The IC50 is measured by in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP
source: These data indicate that the i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited not only from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP, but the drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can also directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition, in addition to its recruitment of more P-TEFb to the MYC locus.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of co-immunoprecipitation and in vitro kinase assays.

claim: The drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition
source: These data indicate that the i-CDK9-mediated MYC induction benefited not only from efficient release of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP, but the drug-enhanced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction can also directly promote CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition, in addition to its recruitment of more P-TEFb to the MYC locus.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vitro kinase assays showing BRD4's effects on CDK9 activity and inhibitor sensitivity.

claim: i-CDK9 caused a significant increase in BRD4's occupancy across the entire MYC locus
source: The first noticeable major change caused by i-CDK9 is the significant increase in BRD4's occupancy across the entire MYC locus (Figure 5A,B)
evidence: The increased occupancy is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figures 5A and 5B.

claim: There was significantly elevated CDK9 binding to the MYC locus upon i-CDK9 treatment
source: Correlating with this increase and consistent with the i-CDK9-induced BRD4-P-TEFb interaction, there was also significantly elevated CDK9 binding to the MYC locus (Figure 5B).
evidence: The elevated binding is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B.

claim: The elevation in CDK9 binding to the MYC locus was mostly BRD4 dependent
source: Although the elevation in CDK9 binding was mostly BRD4 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The BRD4 dependence is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution pattern of CDK9 was somewhat different from that of BRD4 at the MYC locus
source: the distribution pattern of CDK9 was somewhat different from that of BRD4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The different distribution patterns are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B.

claim: The difference in distribution patterns between CDK9 and BRD4 could be caused by P-TEFb's dissociation from BRD4 and joining the Pol II elongation complex once it is recruited to the MYC chromatin template
source: This difference could be caused by P-TEFb's dissociation from BRD4 and joining the Pol II elongation complex once it is recruited to the MYC chromatin template.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed distribution differences.

claim: i-CDK9 markedly enhanced the concentration of Pol II across the entire MYC locus
source: Consistent with the demonstration that the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression is due to increased transcription by Pol II (Figure 3A,F), i-CDK9 also markedly enhanced the concentration of Pol II across the entire MYC locus (Figure 5B).
evidence: The enhanced Pol II occupancy is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B.

claim: Despite incubation with 0.3 μM i-CDK9 for 8 hr, the pSer2 level still increased at the MYC locus
source: Furthermore, despite the incubation with 0.3 μM i-CDK9 for 8 hr, a condition that was shown above to decrease the global Ser2 phosphorylation on Pol II CTD by about 40% (Figure 3B), the pSer2 level was found to still increase at the MYC locus (Figure 5B).
evidence: The increased pSer2 at the MYC locus is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B, despite global decrease shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The pSer2 distribution shifted toward the 3′ end of the MYC gene compared to CDK9 and total Pol II
source: Comparing to CDK9 and total Pol II, the pSer2 distribution shifted toward the 3′ end of the gene, which is consistent with the patterns detected on many other actively transcribed genes (Rahl et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: The distribution pattern is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5B and is consistent with patterns reported in the literature.

claim: On HEXIM1, i-CDK9 treatment decreased the levels of both total Pol II and Pol II with pSer2 CTD
source: In contrast to the situation observed on the i-CDK9-induced MYC gene, on HEXIM1, a gene that was permanently inhibited by i-CDK9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), the same treatment decreased the levels of both total Pol II and Pol II with pSer2 CTD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The decreased Pol II levels are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The levels of acetylated histones H3 and H4 in whole cell extracts remained unchanged upon exposure to i-CDK9
source: Finally, while the levels of acetylated histones H3 (Ac-H3) and H4 (Ac-H4) in whole cell extracts remained unchanged upon exposure to i-CDK9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The unchanged levels are shown by Western blotting in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Acetylated histones H3 and H4 increased across the MYC locus especially at locations surrounding the major P1 promoter upon i-CDK9 treatment
source: they were found to increase across the MYC locus especially at locations surrounding the major P1 promoter (Figure 5C).
evidence: The increased acetylation is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5C.

claim: The increase in acetylated histones at the MYC locus explains the drug-promoted BRD4 binding to the MYC locus
source: Although the underlying mechanism for this increase is unclear, it explains well the drug-promoted BRD4 binding to the MYC locus.
evidence: This is an inference based on BRD4's known function as a reader of acetylated histones.

claim: At early time points of i-CDK9 treatment (0, 1 and 2 hr) when MYC transcription was yet to be induced, the acetylation state of the MYC promoter was already different from that of the HEXIM1 promoter
source: Interestingly, even at early time points of i-CDK9 treatment (0, 1 and 2 hr) when MYC transcription was yet to be induced, the acetylation state of the MYC promoter was already different from that of the HEXIM1 promoter.
evidence: This observation is based on ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The levels of both Ac-H3 and Ac-H4 at the MYC promoter began to increase at early stages of i-CDK9 treatment, with the more robust increase observed for Ac-H4
source: As shown in Figure 5D, the levels of both Ac-H3 and Ac-H4 at the MYC promoter began to increase at this early stage, with the more robust increase observed for Ac-H4.
evidence: The early increases are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: At the HEXIM1 promoter, i-CDK9 caused a drastic decrease in the Ac-H3 level but a small increase of Ac-H4
source: In contrast, at the HEXIM1 promoter, i-CDK9 caused a drastic decrease in the Ac-H3 level but a small increase of Ac-H4.
evidence: The differential changes are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: BRD4 level displayed a marked decrease at the MYC promoter at 1 hr post i-CDK9 treatment, but began to rebound by 2 hr
source: As for the BRD4 level, it displayed a marked decrease at the MYC promoter at 1 hr post i-CDK9 treatment, but began to rebound by 2 hr.
evidence: The temporal changes in BRD4 level are shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: At the HEXIM1 promoter, BRD4 showed a sustained reduction throughout the entire early period of i-CDK9 treatment
source: At the HEXIM1 promoter, however, it showed a sustained reduction throughout the entire period (Figure 5D).
evidence: The sustained reduction is shown by ChIP-qPCR in Figure 5D.

claim: Early differences at the chromatin level predispose a transiently repressed gene such as MYC and a permanently repressed one such as HEXIM1 to completely different expression states later on during the i-CDK9 treatment
source: It is likely that these early differences at the chromatin level predispose a transiently repressed gene such as MYC and a permanently repressed one such as HEXIM1 to completely different expression states later on during the i-CDK9 treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the early chromatin differences observed between MYC and HEXIM1.

claim: The i-CDK9-induced MYC expression is likely caused by a combination of: (1) the induced transfer of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to BRD4; (2) BRD4's promotion of CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition; and (3) favorable chromatin changes at an early stage of the i-CDK9 treatment
source: Taken together, the data presented thus far indicate that the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression is likely caused by a combination of events: (1) the induced transfer of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to BRD4; (2) BRD4's promotion of CDK9's kinase activity and resistance to inhibition; and (3) favorable chromatin changes at an early stage of the i-CDK9 treatment that lead to subsequent increase in the occupancy of the BRD4-P-TEFb complex at the MYC locus, promotion of Ser2 phosphorylation on the Pol II CTD, and finally productive transcriptional elongation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the mechanistic data presented in the study.

claim: MYC is a classic example of primary response genes (PRGs)
source: MYC is a classic example of the so-called PRGs, which are a set of genes that can be induced in response to both extracellular and intracellular signals without the requirement for de novo protein synthesis (Fowler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Fowler et al., 2011.

claim: Primary response genes can be induced in response to both extracellular and intracellular signals without the requirement for de novo protein synthesis
source: MYC is a classic example of the so-called PRGs, which are a set of genes that can be induced in response to both extracellular and intracellular signals without the requirement for de novo protein synthesis (Fowler et al., 2011).
evidence: This is the definition of PRGs with citation to Fowler et al., 2011.

claim: At the 2-hr time point, GSEA reveals a marked i-CDK9-induced reduction of expression (NES = −2.28) for essentially all the 27 BDPR genes
source: At the 2-hr time point, GSEA reveals a marked i-CDK9-induced reduction of expression (normalized enrichment score or NES = −2.28) for essentially all the 27 genes within the gene set (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The GSEA results are shown in Figure 6B.

claim: At the 8-hr time point, virtually all the BDPR genes displayed significant up-regulation by i-CDK9 (NES = +2.26)
source: However, at the 8-hr time point, the trend was completely reversed with virtually all the genes displaying significant up-regulation by i-CDK9 (Figure 6C; NES = +2.26).
evidence: The GSEA results are shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The biphasic transcriptional signature of the curated BDPR genes is the same as that of MYC in their response to i-CDK9
source: Thus, the biphasic transcriptional signature of the curated BDPR genes is the same as that of MYC in their response to i-CDK9.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the GSEA results for BDPR genes with the MYC expression pattern.

claim: The 23 BDPR genes with detectable Pol II ChIP-seq signals in HeLa cells showed little change in their Pol II TR values after exposure to i-CDK9 for 8 hr
source: Another interesting observation about the 23 BDPR genes that had detectable Pol II ChIP-seq signals in HeLa cells (Figure 6A, bold face type) is that they showed little change in their Pol II TR values after the exposure to i-CDK9 for 8 hr (Figure 6D).
evidence: The TR values are shown by ChIP-seq analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: A significant increase in TR was found for most of the remaining or 23 randomly selected genes in the ChIP-seq database after i-CDK9 treatment
source: In contrast, a significant increase in TR was found for most of the remaining (Figure 6D upper panel) or 23 randomly selected genes (lower panel) in the ChIP-seq database.
evidence: The TR changes are shown by ChIP-seq analysis in Figure 6D.

claim: i-CDK9 caused a significant and fairly uniform increase in Pol II occupancy across the entire length of MYC, FOS, and JUNB genes
source: A close examination of the distribution patterns of Pol II on three well-studied PRGs, MYC, FOS, and JUNB, which happen to be highly important proto-oncogenes, reveals that i-CDK9 caused a significant and fairly uniform increase in Pol II occupancy across the entire length of these genes (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The Pol II distribution is shown by ChIP-seq in Figures 6E-G.

claim: The distribution of Pol II on MYC as revealed by ChIP-seq is remarkably similar to that obtained by the classic ChIP-qPCR
source: Notably, the distribution of Pol II on MYC as revealed by ChIP-seq is remarkably similar to that obtained by the classic ChIP-qPCR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This comparison validates the consistency between two different ChIP methods.

claim: The uniform increase in Pol II occupancy across BDPR genes explains why their TR values underwent little change
source: These results are not only consistent with the induced expression of these genes by i-CDK9, but also explain why their TR values underwent little change in the process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the definition of TR and the observed uniform Pol II increase.

claim: The induced transfer of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to BRD4 and the BRD4-mediated protection and enhancement of P-TEFb's activity and recruitment to chromatin templates are the primary driving force behind the induction of MYC and other BDPR genes by i-CDK9
source: Taken in aggregate, the data so far strongly support the notion that the induced transfer of P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to BRD4 and the BRD4-mediated protection and enhancement of P-TEFb's activity and recruitment to chromatin templates are the primary driving force behind the induction of MYC and other BDPR genes by i-CDK9.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the mechanistic data on BDPR genes.

claim: MYC knockdown markedly reduced pSer2 levels in both untreated cells as well as in cells exposed to a range of i-CDK9 concentrations
source: Indeed, even though the KD was incomplete, it markedly reduced pSer2 levels in both untreated cells as well as in cells exposed to a range of i-CDK9 concentrations (Figure 7A)
evidence: The effect of MYC knockdown is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7A.

claim: MYC is required for CDK9 to phosphorylate the Pol II CTD under both normal and inhibitory conditions
source: Indeed, even though the KD was incomplete, it markedly reduced pSer2 levels in both untreated cells as well as in cells exposed to a range of i-CDK9 concentrations (Figure 7A), revealing a requirement of MYC for CDK9 to phosphorylate the Pol II CTD under both normal and inhibitory conditions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MYC knockdown experiment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: JQ1 slightly decreased the cellular pSer2 levels
source: Not only did the KD of MYC expression negatively affect the ability of CDK9 to phosphorylate Ser2, the treatment of cells with either JQ1, the BET bromodomain inhibitor that suppressed the BRD4-dependent MYC expression (Figure 4C), or 10,058-F4, a small molecule inhibitor that inhibits the MYC-MAX interaction to prevent transactivation of genes targeted by this heterodimer (Rahl et al., 2010), also slightly decreased the cellular pSer2 levels (Figure 7B, lane 4; Figure 7C, lane 2).
evidence: The decrease is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7B.

claim: 10,058-F4 slightly decreased the cellular pSer2 levels
source: Not only did the KD of MYC expression negatively affect the ability of CDK9 to phosphorylate Ser2, the treatment of cells with either JQ1, the BET bromodomain inhibitor that suppressed the BRD4-dependent MYC expression (Figure 4C), or 10,058-F4, a small molecule inhibitor that inhibits the MYC-MAX interaction to prevent transactivation of genes targeted by this heterodimer (Rahl et al., 2010), also slightly decreased the cellular pSer2 levels (Figure 7B, lane 4; Figure 7C, lane 2).
evidence: The decrease is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7C.

claim: When JQ1 was used in combination with i-CDK9, global pSer2 dropped to levels that were much lower than those caused by i-CDK9 alone
source: More importantly, when JQ1 or 10,058-F4 was used in combination with i-CDK9, global pSer2 dropped to levels that were much lower than those caused by i-CDK9 alone (Figure 7B, lane 3; Figure 7C, lane 4).
evidence: The synergistic decrease is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7B.

claim: When 10,058-F4 was used in combination with i-CDK9, global pSer2 dropped to levels that were much lower than those caused by i-CDK9 alone
source: More importantly, when JQ1 or 10,058-F4 was used in combination with i-CDK9, global pSer2 dropped to levels that were much lower than those caused by i-CDK9 alone (Figure 7B, lane 3; Figure 7C, lane 4).
evidence: The synergistic decrease is shown by Western blotting in Figure 7C.

claim: MYC normally functions to facilitate P-TEFb's phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD on Ser2
source: All together, these results are consistent with the idea that MYC normally functions to facilitate P-TEFb's phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD on Ser2 and that decreasing the expression or activity of MYC eliminates this beneficial effect.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of MYC knockdown and inhibitor experiments.

claim: Decreasing the expression or activity of MYC eliminates the beneficial effect of MYC on P-TEFb's phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD
source: All together, these results are consistent with the idea that MYC normally functions to facilitate P-TEFb's phosphorylation of the Pol II CTD on Ser2 and that decreasing the expression or activity of MYC eliminates this beneficial effect.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the combined results of MYC knockdown and inhibitor experiments.

claim: MYC can bind and recruit P-TEFb to numerous MYC-target genes to activate transcription
source: The observation that MYC can bind and recruit P-TEFb to numerous MYC-target genes to activate transcription (Kanazawa et al., 2003; Rahl et al., 2010) provides a plausible explanation for its promotion of P-TEFb's pSer2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Kanazawa et al., 2003 and Rahl et al., 2010.

claim: The amounts of CDK9, CycT1, and BRD4 bound to the immunoprecipitated MYC-F increased upon exposure to i-CDK9
source: Indeed, the amounts of CDK9, CycT1, and BRD4 bound to the immunoprecipitated MYC-F were found to increase upon the exposure to i-CDK9 (Figure 7D,E)
evidence: The increased binding is shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: Cells use a dual mechanism to compensate for the loss of CDK9 activity by targeting the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to essential genes via a MYC-dependent pathway
source: Indeed, the amounts of CDK9, CycT1, and BRD4 bound to the immunoprecipitated MYC-F were found to increase upon the exposure to i-CDK9 (Figure 7D,E), revealing a dual mechanism used by cells to compensate for the loss of CDK9 activity by targeting the BRD4-P-TEFb complex to essential genes via a MYC-dependent pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the increased MYC-P-TEFb interaction upon i-CDK9 treatment.

claim: The combination of i-CDK9 and JQ1 synergistically inhibited growth of both HeLa and H1792 cell lines
source: Our data clearly show that the combination of i-CDK9 and JQ1 synergistically inhibited growth of both cell lines (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: The synergistic inhibition is shown by isobologram analysis in Figures 7F and 7G.

claim: The combination of i-CDK9 and JQ1 synergistically induced apoptosis of both HeLa and H1792 cells as demonstrated by Caspase 3/7 production
source: In addition to inhibition of cell growth, the combination of i-CDK9 and JQ1 also synergistically induced apoptosis of both HeLa and H1792 cells as demonstrated by isobolograms that measure the production of Caspase 3/7 in treated cells (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: The synergistic apoptosis induction is shown by isobologram analysis in Figures 7H and 7I.

claim: Strong and synergistic apoptosis caused by i-CDK9 and JQ1 was observed by flow cytometry measurement of propidium iodide (PI)-stained sub-G1 population of HeLa cells
source: Furthermore, strong and synergistic apoptosis caused by i-CDK9 and JQ1 was also observed by flow cytometry measurement of propidium iodide (PI)-stained sub-G1 population of HeLa cells that contained fragmented DNA (Figure 7J).
evidence: The synergistic apoptosis is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7J.

claim: The MYC inhibitor 10,058-F4 synergized with i-CDK9 to induce potent cell death
source: Finally, in addition of JQ1, the MYC inhibitor 10,058-F4 was also found to synergize with i-CDK9 to induce potent cell death (Figure 7K).
evidence: The synergistic cell death is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 7K.

claim: Simultaneous inhibition of CDK9's kinase activity and MYC's expression or function leads to synergistic induction of growth arrest and apoptosis of cancer cells
source: Taken all together, the data are consistent with the notion that simultaneous inhibition of CDK9's kinase activity and MYC's expression or function leads to synergistic induction of growth arrest and apoptosis of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the combination treatment experiments.

claim: CDK9 is the kinase subunit of positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb)
source: CDK9 is the kinase subunit of positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) that enables RNA polymerase (Pol) II's transition from promoter-proximal pausing to productive elongation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: P-TEFb enables RNA polymerase (Pol) II's transition from promoter-proximal pausing to productive elongation
source: CDK9 is the kinase subunit of positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) that enables RNA polymerase (Pol) II's transition from promoter-proximal pausing to productive elongation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: i-CDK9 potently suppresses CDK9 phosphorylation of substrates
source: Here, we describe the development of i-CDK9 as such an inhibitor that potently suppresses CDK9 phosphorylation of substrates and causes genome-wide Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: i-CDK9 causes genome-wide Pol II pausing
source: Here, we describe the development of i-CDK9 as such an inhibitor that potently suppresses CDK9 phosphorylation of substrates and causes genome-wide Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: While most genes experience reduced expression upon i-CDK9 treatment, MYC and other primary response genes increase expression upon sustained i-CDK9 treatment
source: While most genes experience reduced expression, MYC and other primary response genes increase expression upon sustained i-CDK9 treatment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: BRD4 captures P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to deliver to target genes
source: Essential for this increase, the bromodomain protein BRD4 captures P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to deliver to target genes and also enhances CDK9's activity and resistance to inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: BRD4 enhances CDK9's activity and resistance to inhibition
source: Essential for this increase, the bromodomain protein BRD4 captures P-TEFb from 7SK snRNP to deliver to target genes and also enhances CDK9's activity and resistance to inhibition.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings in the abstract.

claim: The i-CDK9-induced MYC expression and binding to P-TEFb compensate for P-TEFb's loss of activity
source: Because the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression and binding to P-TEFb compensate for P-TEFb's loss of activity, only simultaneously inhibiting CDK9 and MYC/BRD4 can efficiently induce growth arrest and apoptosis of cancer cells
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings and their implications in the abstract.

claim: Only simultaneously inhibiting CDK9 and MYC/BRD4 can efficiently induce growth arrest and apoptosis of cancer cells
source: Because the i-CDK9-induced MYC expression and binding to P-TEFb compensate for P-TEFb's loss of activity, only simultaneously inhibiting CDK9 and MYC/BRD4 can efficiently induce growth arrest and apoptosis of cancer cells, suggesting the potential of a combinatorial treatment strategy.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings and their implications in the abstract.
